awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Investigating the gut microbiome’s impact on fiber digestibility
awd_abstract_narration:
Fiber is a type of carbohydrate that is difficult to digest and fiber-rich diets can present nutrient absorption challenges. Several evolutionary adaptations that maximize fiber digestibility (e.g., slow gut passage time and/ or microbial fermentation) have been identified in non-human primates. However, while it is known that the microbiome converts fiber into short-chain fatty acids, its adaptive role in fiber digestibility is poorly understood. This doctoral dissertation project examines the role of the gut microbiome in fiber digestibility in three non-human primate species, contributing to our growing understanding of microbiome adaptations and functions. The study is also relevant for understanding non-human primate survival and reproduction, conservation initiatives, and captive animal care. The study promotes community engaged research and conservation education.  

This doctoral dissertation research evaluates fiber digestibility across three non-human primate species that have different feeding strategies in the wild. The study collects data on behavior/feeding, plant samples, and feces to measure fiber input and output, fiber digestibility, and the functional role of the gut microbiome.  Fecal samples are analyzed using 'shotgun' metagenomic sequencing to profile the composition and function of the gut microbiome across species and between seasons. By combining methods from nutritional ecology and microbiome research, the study expands current knowledge of primate ecology and evolution, directly informing ongoing conservation efforts.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project focused on understanding how fiber is digested by lemur species with different feeding specializations (Propithecus diadema - leaf-eater, Eulemur fulvus - fruit-eater, and Hapalemur griseus - bamboo specialist) during the resource-abundant and lean seasons. Focal follows were conducted for 4 weeks during two field seasons: one in the dry/lean season (September 2024) and one in the rainy/abundant season (February 2024). Behavioral and feeding data alongside fecal samples were collected to measure fiber digestibility and describe the gut microbiome of these lemur species. 172 plant foods consumed by these lemurs were collected to measure fiber input and 112 fecal samples were collected to measure fiber output, giving an estimate of fiber digestibility. Though fiber digestibility estimates are still being calculated, preliminary data on the  fiber content of foods shows that fiber content differs across the three different lemur species but not significantly across the two seasons. 123 fecal samples were collected to describe the composition and function of the gut microbiome and determine how it is supporting fiber digestion in these lemurs during these two seasons. Preliminary data shows clear differences in the composition and function of the gut microbiome across species or dietary specialization and significant differences across both seasons for each species.

 To help uplift Malagasy communities in primate research, multiple opportunities and outreach programs were included in this project. PI Gherardi worked with two Malagasy graduate students, Nyony mamy koloina Rakotoarivelo and Sarah Rajaonarivelo, who took on the roles of team leaders to collect data for this research project while also supporting data collection for their graduate research. This project employed over 20 research technicians, including new research technicians who were trained on behavioral data and fecal collection methods. Professional development opportunities were provided to Malagasy graduate students at the University of Antananarivo through workshops in preparation for the International Primatological Society conference held in Madagascar in July 2025. A community outreach weekend was organized by PI Gherardi and Malagasy graduate students to help educate local families on the importance of lemurs and conservation in Madagascar, with 172 children participating. This entailed taking a trip to the forest to see the lemurs, card games, trivia, a coloring competition, reading books about protecting the environment and Madagascar's unique biodiversity, and documentaries on sustainable agriculture. A survey was also conducted with the help of 6 Malagasy graduate students to assess knowledge of lemurs, conservation, and biodiversity by local children. Working collaboratively with local secondary teachers, PI Gherardi and the Malagasy team provided supplies for the students and classroom and helped start a conservation club to promote local stewardship of the environment. Additionally, PI Gherardi 3D printed models of lemur skulls to demonstrate the wide diversity of lemur species in Madagascar and contributed this to the NGO Sadabe to start a small, local natural history museum and use these models as learning tools for the local people in Tsinjoarivo.

Final analyses and results of the project are anticipated to be completed in Fall 2026 by PI Gherardi. Future findings from this project have the potential to greatly expand our understanding of nutrient absorption, specifically fiber digestion, and the evolution of feeding strategies in primates. This research has implications for conservation, providing information that can help inform future reforestation and restoration projects, make predictions about the adaptability of primate species to habitat and climate change, and develop species-specific diets to better care for captive populations of primates.
